target_audience: University students or advanced high school students familiar with basic calculus

sections.title: The Shift: From Slope to Stretching
lecture_lines: Traditionally, we see derivatives as slopes on graphs.
Let's view them as dynamic transformations instead.
Functions map an input space to an output space.
animations: Display title "The Shift: From Slope to Stretching" in #FFFFFF and a simple slope visualization [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/slope.svg].
Fade out slope, display parallel lines "Input" (#00FF00) and "Output" (#00BFFF).
Draw mapping arrows from Input points to Output points to show transformation.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Functions as Mappings
lecture_lines: Imagine two parallel lines for input and output.
Arrows show how input points map to output points.
This shifts focus from coordinates to relative lengths.
animations: Display two parallel horizontal lines labeled "Input" (#00FF00) and "Output" (#00BFFF).
Draw multiple arrows (#FFFFFF) connecting Input values to their mapped Output values.
Highlight a segment on Input and its image on Output to emphasize length change.

sections.title: Defining the Local Scaling Factor
lecture_lines: Focus on a tiny interval, dx, around a point.
The function maps dx to output interval df.
The derivative is the local scaling factor.
Here, df equals the derivative times dx.
Scaling factor determines if intervals stretch or shrink.
animations: Highlight a small segment labeled "dx" (#FFFF00) on the Input line (#00FF00).
Show the corresponding mapped segment "df" (#FF0000) on the Output line (#00BFFF).
Display formula "df \approx f'(x) \cdot dx" in #FFFFFF while highlighting both segments.
Transform "df" to be 3x the length of "dx" with label "f'(x) = 3".
Transform "df" to be 0.5x the length of "dx" with label "f'(x) = 0.5".

sections.title: Visualizing Non-Linear Transformation (f(x) = x²)
lecture_lines: Observe the transformation for the function x squared.
At x equals one, the scaling factor is two.
At x equals three, the scaling increases to six.
The stretching power changes across the input line.
Larger inputs result in much more intense stretching.
animations: Show "f(x) = x^2" in #FFFFFF; highlight dx at x=1 on Input (#00FF00).
Show mapped df on Output (#00BFFF) with a 2x stretch relative to dx.
Highlight dx at x=3 on Input; show mapped df with a 6x stretch on Output.
Animate a gradient #FF4500 across Input to represent the varying "stretching power".
Illustrate high-density stretching at x=3 by zooming in on the Output line.

sections.title: Conclusion: Sensitivity and Density
lecture_lines: Derivatives measure output sensitivity to input changes.
High derivatives spread points out in the output.
Low derivatives pack points closer together.
animations: Display "Sensitivity" in #FFFF00 and highlight the Output line's response to Input.
Show points spreading out on Output for a large derivative visualization.
Show points clustering together on Output for a small derivative visualization.
